MBE Growth of Superconductors.title: Architecture-driven optical redshift and photoconductive response in In/Ga nitride digital heterostructures
MBE Growth of Superconductors.authors: Eduardo F. Fernández, Manuel Peralta-Fuentes, Álvaro Valera-Albacete, Aykut Can Önel, Yasemin Tabak, Florencia Almonacid Cruz
MBE Growth of Superconductors.abstract: Accessing low-energy optical transitions in c-axis III-nitrides remains challenging because high indium incorporation is constrained by lattice mismatch, thermal instability, strain, and compositional inhomogeneity. Here, we investigate shutter-defined In/Ga nitride digital architectures (DAs) grown by plasma-assisted molecular beam epitaxy as an alternative route for modifying the optical response without relying solely on conventional random-alloy composition control. High-resolution x-ray diffraction (XRD) reveals architecture-dependent structural modulation within a predominantly GaN-like framework, with no secondary crystalline phases detectable by XRD. The optical response varies strongly with the digital architecture; the shortest-period structure exhibits a reflectance-derived effective optical transition energy of approximately 2.24 eV, substantially below that of the GaN reference. Pronounced Fabry–Pérot oscillations further indicate sufficiently uniform optical thickness to sustain multiple-beam interference. Under 405 nm illumination, the same architecture exhibits a reproducible light-induced reduction in resistance and a seconds-scale post-illumination recovery. These results demonstrate that shutter-defined In/Ga nitride DAs provide a promising route for engineering low-energy optical transitions and the photoconductive response within the c-axis III-nitride platform.

MBE Growth of Superconductors.title: Influences of $N_2$ flow rate on the superconducting properties and dimensionality of epitaxial TiN thin films
MBE Growth of Superconductors.authors: Shilong Chen, Yuchuan Liu, Yihui Sun, Xiaoni Wang, Wei Peng, Yu Wu, Gang Mu, Zhirong Lin
MBE Growth of Superconductors.abstract: TiN thin films have received great attention in the field of superconducting quantum computing due to their low loss characteristics derived from stable chemical and thermal properties, as well as excellent electrical conductivity. In this study, TiN thin films with a thickness of 35 nm were epitaxially grown on MgO substrates using the DC reactive magnetron sputtering technique. The crystal structure, film thickness, and surface morphology of the thin films were characterized. The films exhibit a very flat surface with a root mean square roughness of only a few tenths of a nanometer. The influences of nitrogen ($N_2$) flow rate on the surface morphology, superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$), residual resistivity ratio (RRR), normal-state resistivity ($ρ_n$), upper critical field, and superconducting dimensionality were investigated systematically. The experimental results show that the TiN film deposited with a $N_2$ flow rate of 1.5 sccm exhibits optimal performance, including the highest $T_c$ (4.93 K), the largest RRR, the lowest $ρ_n$, and the lowest slope of the out-of-film upper critical field near Tc. Moreover, it is found that the background vacuum inside the growth chamber has a significant impact on the superconducting properties of TiN films, and the degradation of vacuum degree can lead to the decrease of $T_c$. The upper critical field reveals a significant anisotropic feature. Importantly, the in-film upper critical field data demonstrates that the optimization of sample quality leads to deviation from two-dimensional superconducting behavior, which provides a new perspective on the influencing factors of superconducting dimensionality beyond the thickness of films. The present results provide useful references for a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between growth parameters and the superconducting properties of thin films.

Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.title: Nonlinear Hall Effect in a Semiconductor Heterostructure with Rashba and Dresselhaus Effects
Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.authors: Jeong Ung Ahn, Junyeong Choi, Minseong Kwon, Won-Young Choi, Ki Hyuk Han, Cheol Jun Kim, Chaun Jang, Dong-Soo Han, OukJae Lee, Byoung-Chul Min, Kyoung-Whan Kim, Hyun Cheol Koo
Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.abstract: We report a nonlinear Hall effect in a high-mobility InAs quantum-well two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG) with coexisting Rashba and Dresselhaus spin–orbit interactions. Under zero magnetic field, a second-harmonic transverse electric field emerges that scales quadratically with current density and is significantly larger than the second-harmonic longitudinal response. Angle-dependent measurements reveal a pronounced 2-fold anisotropy that follows the combined spin–orbit field. This 2-fold symmetry reflects the anisotropic spin–orbit field generated by coexisting Rashba and Dresselhaus interactions rather than crystal symmetry. The normalized signal reaches ∼10–9 V–1 m and persists up to room temperature. Conductivity scaling shows a quadratic dependence consistent with skew-scattering-dominated transport. These results establish conventional semiconductor 2DEGs as a promising platform for spin-orbit-driven nonlinear transport and rectification functionalities.

Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.title: Interfacial Schottky-barrier-assisted optoelectronic resistive switching and synaptic plasticity in ITO/BiFeO3/ZnO/BiFeO3/Ag heterostructure memristors
Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.authors: Jian Peng, Jie Zhang, Shunping Shi, Chuanyu Zhang, Yong Zhao
Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.abstract: An ITO/BiFeO3/ZnO/BiFeO3/Ag heterostructure memristor was fabricated by magnetron sputtering and post-annealing to investigate Schottky-barrier-assisted resistive switching and synaptic plasticity. Structural characterization confirms the formation of a compact BiFeO3/ZnO/BiFeO3 multilayer film with nanocrystalline morphology and distinct ZnO and BiFeO3 phases. The device exhibits stable bipolar resistive switching, and illumination enhances the resistance-state separation by modulating carrier concentration and oxygen-vacancy-related defect states. Transport analysis indicates Ohmic conduction at low bias, while Schottky emission dominates the higher-bias region, revealing the important role of BiFeO3/ZnO interfacial barriers. The switching behavior is primarily associated with oxygen-vacancy-assisted conductive pathway formation and rupture, while reversible Schottky barrier modulation at the heterointerfaces further regulates carrier transport. Furthermore, illumination- and pulse-interval-dependent long-term potentiation and depression are demonstrated, revealing optically tunable synaptic plasticity. These results suggest that the BiFeO3/ZnO/BiFeO3 heterostructure provides an effective platform for optoelectronic memristors and artificial synaptic devices.

Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.title: Fe:Ge flux-ratio-dependent phase evolution and magnetic transport in Fe3GeTe2 thin films grown on GaAs(111)
Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms. II. Adsorption of nonmetal atoms (N, P, As, and Sb) on Ga-terminated surfaces
Superconductor-Semiconductor Interfaces.abstract: Ab initio calculations were used to simulate the adsorption processes on Ga-terminated surfaces of tetrahedral semiconductors: GaN, GaP, GaAs and GaSb. The considered adsorbates are nonmetal species, i.e., nitrogen, phosphorus, arsenic, and antimony on wurtzite gallium nitride, i.e., GaN(0001) surfaces, zinc blende gallium phosphide, i.e., GaP(111), gallium arsenide, GaAs(111), and gallium antimonide, GaSb (111) surfaces. The cases investigated include single adsorbed nonmetal atoms and full coverage, i.e. theta=1 of these surfaces. The calculated results include the stable sites and the energies of the single adsorbed atoms: located at H3 sites at low coverage and in on-top positions at high coverage for GaP, GaAs and GaSb. At high nitrogen coverage, the N2 admolecules are formed, weakly attached to the surface. The calculated electronic properties of the single-adatom systems include the band diagrams of the slabs in real and momentum space, the energies of the quantum states. In addition, the overlaps of the quantum states of the nonmetal adatoms and the nearest topmost surface Ga atoms are given. The full coverage data include the atomic configurations and the bond energies of the adsorbed layers. The electronic properties include the above-mentioned data for single adatoms, together with additional properties related to interactions between adsorbed atoms. The evaporation stability analysis confirms that the adatoms stabilize the topmost Ga atoms against detachment because of the high energy barrier of DE > 3 eV which is further increased to DE > 4 eV by coverage located at H3 sites. Thus, growth simulations should employ unreconstructed Ga-terminated surfaces covered by nonmetal atoms located at on-top positions.

Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.title: Growth and morphology of core-shell nanowires incorporating dissimilar hexagonal semiconductors: the case of InAs-ZnTe
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.authors: Danylo Mosiiets, Susheng Tan, Sergey Frolov, Moïra Hocevar, Joel Cibert, Edith Bellet-Amalric
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.abstract: Core-shell nanowires incorporating semiconductors from two groups, III-V for the core and II-VI for the shell, have been grown by molecular beam epitaxy in two dedicated chambers connected under ultra-high vacuum, and studied by electron microscopy. During the growth of the shell, the wurtzite structure of the core is replicated in the shell, without any creation of defects. This is true for a wide range of shell thickness, from about one monolayer, up to 25 nm thanks to the good lattice match between the InAs material of the core and the ZnTe material of the shell. While (1 100) m-facets and (11 20) a-facets coexist on the sidewalls of the core, during the growth of the ZnTe shell the size of the m-facets progressively increases at the expense of the a-facets which eventually disappear. A fast growth of the ZnTe shell is observed for the first few monolayers, with a high sticking; this is followed by a slower growth, of the same order of magnitude as observed on a ZnTe core, with a dependence on the nanowire radius which points to the occurrence of mononuclear nucleation

Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.title: Growth rate and indium incorporation during growth of InGaN/GaN quantum well structures in pyramidal micro-LED devices
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.authors: Ivan Martinovic, Chih-Wei Hsu, Eric Tseng, Zahra Mohammadian Rasnani, Lisa Rullik, Per Olof Holtz, Per O. Å. Persson
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.abstract: Pyramidal micro-light emitting diodes (μLEDs) based on five InGaN/GaN quantum well (QW) pairs were synthesized via selective area growth in a metal-organic chemical vapor deposition system. Electroluminescence, optical microscopy, and cathodoluminescence (CL) were used to study the emission properties of the pyramidal μLEDs. The QW emission from the pyramidal structures reaches shorter wavelengths with increasing bias, which can be ascribed to the subsequent activation of InGaN QWs with increasing bandgaps. According to CL and plan-view scanning transmission electron microscopy, the longer emission wavelengths correlate spatially with increasing indium content associated with the pyramid ridges. Further imaging and elemental mapping of the QWs near the pyramid ridges reveal that adjacent QWs interface through a trench, situated precisely along the ridge between facets, wherein the QWs are thicker and the In content is enhanced. It is inferred that both parameters are induced by a higher growth rate in the trenches. The herein presented results provide a detailed view of how In incorporation and hence the emission properties are affected by the different growth rates that occur through geometrical variations in pyramidal μLEDs.

Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.title: Size and temperature effect on Young's modulus of silicon nanowires
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.authors: Guangming Cheng, Tzu-Hsuan Chang, Hongyu Wang, Yong Zhu
Nanowire Selective Area and Template-Ass.abstract: This paper reports quantitative measurements of the Young's modulus of 78 silicon nanowires (SiNWs) with diameters ranging from 20 to 160 nm over a temperature range from room temperature to 600 K. The SiNWs were synthesized using the vapor–liquid–solid growth process, with a ⟨112⟩ growth direction and a single twin boundary running parallel to the nanowire axis. Uniaxial tensile tests were performed at multiple temperatures using a microelectromechanical system-based testing platform inside a transmission electron microscope. A total of 200 Young's modulus measurements were obtained, as most SiNWs were tested at multiple temperatures. At each temperature, the Young's modulus decreases systematically with decreasing nanowire diameter. Furthermore, the Young's modulus exhibits an approximately linear decrease with increasing temperature, and the magnitude of this temperature dependence becomes more pronounced as the nanowire diameter decreases. These results reveal the coupled effects of size and temperature on the elastic properties of SiNWs and provide a comprehensive experimental dataset for understanding and modeling the thermomechanical behavior of semiconductor nanostructures.

Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.title: Colloidal Atomic Layer Deposition on Plasmonic Metal Oxide Nanocrystals
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.authors: M. Wren Berry, Victor Segui Barragan, Sofia A. Shubert-Zuleta, Delia J. Milliron
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.abstract: Colloidal atomic layer deposition (c-ALD) has emerged as a powerful technique for enhancing the functional properties of nanocrystals (NCs) while preserving their solution dispersibility. Previous studies have shown that the deposition of amorphous metal oxide shells via c-ALD can passivate surface states in NCs, resulting in improved stability, photoluminescence, conductivity, and energy transfer. However, its application to doped metal oxide NCs, such as tin-doped indium oxide (ITO), which exhibit surface depletion due to surface hydroxyls, remains unexplored. In this work, we implement a c-ALD strategy using ligand-modified precursors to grow amorphous Al2O3, TiO2, and Ga2O3 shells on ITO NCs. We reveal how these coatings influence the plasmonic response and mitigate surface depletion, which we ascribe to surface state passivation. Energy-dependent X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) reveals a reduction in band bending, indicating a modification of the near-surface electronic structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that control over shell thickness enables tunability of the collective plasmonic resonances in assembled ITO NC superlattices. This work expands the scope of c-ALD and establishes a versatile approach for tailoring the optoelectronic properties of doped metal oxide NCs in solution-processable systems.

Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.title: Atomic Lift-Off of Wafer-Scale Single-Crystalline Gold Membranes Enables Buried-Interface Epitaxy for Flexible Oxide Electronics
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.authors: Yongbin Sun, Hanwen Chi, Ziyue Shen, Kaixin Wang, Fan Zhang, Ni Tu, Tianhao Yang, Wenzhe Niu, Zhizhen Ye, Liping Zhu, Jie Jiang
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.abstract: Flexible oxide electronics require inorganic semiconductors that maintain high-performance under bending, yet scalable approaches to wafer-scale single-crystalline (SC) oxide films and, critically, atomically sharp metal/oxide contacts remain limited. Here, we introduce a buried-interface epitaxy strategy based on atomic lift-off of epitaxial metal films to create atomically defined SC metal/oxide heterostructures in flexible architectures. We fabricate 2-in. freestanding SC Au(111) membranes and employ film-flipping to expose the originally buried Au/Si epitaxial interface as an intrinsically atomically flat growth surface. This converts conventional surface deposition into interface deposition, enabling wafer-scale epitaxial Cu2O(111)/Au with a flat interface. The interface-deposited flexible Cu2O exhibits nearly 2-fold higher carrier mobility and photocurrent, while maintaining stable transport under bending. Flexible Cu2O photocathodes further exhibit 1.6 times higher full-angle light harvesting and 5.6 times higher photocurrent-to-mass metrics compared with rigid counterparts. This work establishes freestanding SC metals as transferable epitaxial templates for flexible oxide electronics and energy devices.

Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.title: Converting a superseded Raith electron beam pattern generator into an unattended Critical Dimension SEM
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.authors: Will Gunn, Han-Hao Cheng, Daniel Peace, Fernando Gottardo, Lachlan Hanrahan, Zachary Degnan, Keith Moulding, Nit Taksatorn, Roger Wepf, Markus Rambach, Andrew G. White
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.abstract: Design-based metrology of academic electron beam lithography (EBL) is bottlenecked by low-throughput imaging. For integrated photonics, where nanometre-scale structural variation can significantly limit device performance, scanning electron microscopy (SEM) is the standard tool for critical dimension (CD) metrology, revealing the structure of devices that is not available from optical measurements. Manual SEM imaging on a wafer-scale is time-intensive, can feature operator-dependent distortions, and yields too few data to reliably close the nanofabrication calibration loop. The following details a methodology that utilises existing hardware in an academic cleanroom: a GDSII-to-SEM software workflow that converts a facility's superseded pattern generator into a CD-SEM for unattended image acquisition and efficient CD and line edge roughness (LER) extraction. This is shown for a Raith eLine Plus, and is expected to be applicable to other pattern generators running Raith's NanoSuite. Presented are results demonstrating its three use cases within a facility: accelerated calibration of two photoresists' process windows; chip-scale metrology of integrated photonic devices to track CD variation; and mass dataset acquisition for convolutional neural network training to predict process distortion. This methodology enables foundry-style, metrology-driven process calibration in academic cleanrooms, generalisable beyond photonics to any EBL nanofabrication that requires nanometre-scale CD control.

Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.title: Numerical modelling of current non-uniformity in braided stacks of tapes
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.authors: Wenzhe Hong, Gianluca De Marzi, Chao Zhou, Gabriele Colombo, Huan Jin, Fang Liu, Huajun Liu, Andrea Masi, Luigi Muzzi, Jinggang Qin
Nanofabrication and Cleanroom Processes.abstract: The performance of REBCO multi-stack cables is crucial for next-generation high-field fusion magnets, it is often limited by uneven current distribution. This study employs a 3D finite-element model based on the weak form of the H-formulation to analyze current non-uniformity within a novel BRAided Stacks of Tapes (BRAST) assembly. The model rigorously accounts for the nonlinear E–J power law of the REBCO material, as well as the effects of inter-tape and terminal resistances. The model’s accuracy is verified experimentally. Simulation results establish a clear hierarchy of stability drivers. First, non-uniform terminal resistance determines the inter- tape current imbalance. Low inter-tape contact resistance has a dual role: it amplifies short-range current imbalances at the cable entry point, leading to increased local current loading, while simultaneously promoting a more uniform longitudinal current distribution within the cable, thereby mitigating current inhomogeneity. Furthermore, the analysis reveals that tape regions with reduced critical current can be the onset of overall stack transition, and that the overall stability of the cable is determined by the minimum current-carrying capacity within the tape stack. This study provides quantitative guidance for controlling terminal resistance uniformity and optimizing contact resistance, thereby improving the stability and robustness of BRAST and similar multi- tape superconducting cable systems.

Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.title: Investigation of the Microstructural and Magnetic Properties of Ni on GeSn Layers
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.authors: Tharundev V, Dushyant Singh, Subha Maity, Vigneshwari S R, Dhammapriy Gayakwad, Shivesh Yadav, Krista R Khiangte
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.abstract: Thermal processing of nickel (Ni) layers on germanium-tin (GeSn) can strongly modify the Ni film and the Ni/GeSn interface within a restricted thermal budget; however, the influence of GeSn crystalline quality on Ni-Ge-Sn interfacial evolution and the magnetic response of the Ni layer remains incompletely understood. Here, Ni (15~nm)/Ge$_{1-x}$Sn$_x$/Ge/Gd$_2$O$_3$/Si(111) heterostructures ($x = 0.08$ and $0.10$) were investigated following rapid thermal annealing at 573 and 973~K for 10~s using X-ray diffraction, pole-figure analysis, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy depth profiling, and temperature- and field-dependent magnetization measurements. Annealing at 573~K preserves the crystallographic texture of Ge$_{0.92}$Sn$_{0.08}$, whereas Ge$_{0.90}$Sn$_{0.10}$ exhibits microtwin formation and reduced structural integrity. Annealing at 973~K, employed as a severe upper-bound thermal reference, causes extensive structural degradation in both heterostructures, with substantially greater deterioration in the higher-Sn sample. XPS depth profiling reveals progressive Ni-Ge-Sn intermixing accompanied by pronounced Sn surface segregation with increasing annealing temperature. Magnetization measurements show coexisting ferromagnetic and superparamagnetic contributions in the as-deposited and 573~K samples, whereas annealing at 973~K strongly suppresses the ferromagnetic response, producing highly unsaturated $M(H)$ loops together with reduced saturation magnetization and coercivity. These magnetic changes are consistent with extensive interfacial alloying and dilution of the metallic Ni layer. This study establishes a direct correlation between GeSn crystalline quality, interfacial diffusion, and magnetic behavior.

Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.title: Control-Noise Trade-offs in Industrially Integrated ${}^{28}\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiGe}$ Spin-1/2 Qubits
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.authors: Leon C. Camenzind, Ik Kyeong Jin, Yi-Hsien Wu, Akito Noiri, Kenta Takeda, Takashi Nakajima, Takashi Kobayashi, Giordano Scappucci, Seigo Tarucha
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.abstract: Scaling silicon spin qubits to fault-tolerant processors requires semiconductor foundry integration, yet it remains unclear how industrial fabrication and dense device integration affect qubit control and noise. Here we study ${}^{28}\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiGe}$ electron spin-1/2 qubits fabricated using Intel's industry-compatible 300 mm process and incorporating micromagnets for electrically driven spin resonance, using a high-performance device fabricated in the RIKEN research cleanroom as a reference. Primitive $π/2$-gate fidelities reach the 99.99% level in the Intel devices, which also exhibit longer idle coherence, weaker low-frequency correlations and reduced qubit-to-qubit variability across several measured characteristics. In the present Intel devices, the micromagnets are integrated inline with the back-end-of-line (BEOL) contact routing, with their separation from the quantum well set through the vertical stack design. Relative to the reference, their larger separation contributes to weaker longitudinal and transverse magnetic-field gradients. The weaker longitudinal gradient suppresses the conversion of charge noise into qubit-frequency fluctuations, whereas the weaker transverse gradient reduces electrically driven spin-resonance efficiency and makes drive-dependent errors relevant at lower Rabi frequencies. Additional BEOL routing and metal levels required for two-dimensional arrays make such placement decisions increasingly consequential when scaling. These results establish an integration-level control-noise trade-off linking micromagnet placement within densely routed layouts to achievable gate performance, while very high-fidelity operation remains possible in industrially fabricated devices.

Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.title: Full-Potential Korringa Kohn Rostoker Study of Structural and Mechanical Properties in SiGeSn Alloys
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.authors: Wasim Raja Mondal, Swarnava Ghosh, Ka-Ming Tam, Markus Eisenbach, Yang Wang, Hanna Terletska
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.abstract: Accurate first-principles descriptions of open, covalently bonded crystal structures remain challenging within conventional Korringa--Kohn--Rostoker (KKR) approaches owing to the spherical approximations commonly employed for the effective crystal potential. Here, we systematically assess the recently developed full-potential KKR (KKR-FP) implementation in the open-source MuST package and demonstrate its applicability to diamond-structured group-IV semiconductors and SiGeSn alloys. Benchmark calculations for diamond-structured Si reveal substantial limitations of the conventional muffin-tin and atomic sphere approximations, whereas KKR-FP accurately reproduces the experimental equilibrium lattice parameter and bulk modulus, yielding 5.433 and 94.9 GPa. The full-potential treatment also recovers the semiconducting character of Si. Further calculations for elemental Ge and Sn establish the applicability of the approach across group-IV materials. Extending this framework to SiGeSn alloys, we investigate their composition-dependent equilibrium lattice parameters, bulk moduli, and mixing enthalpies. The calculated lattice parameters exhibit positive deviations from Vegard's law, while the bulk modulus decreases substantially with changes in alloy composition. Moreover, positive mixing enthalpies of 180.92 and 346.32 meV/atom are obtained for Si0.5Ge0.375Sn0.125 and Si0.375Ge0.25Sn0.375, respectively, indicating an energetic penalty for homogeneous alloy formation relative to the selected elemental reference states. These findings highlight the importance of nonspherical potential contributions in accurately describing open-structured semiconductors and establish KKR-FP within MuST as a promising framework for investigating the structural properties and mixing energetics of compositionally complex group-IV alloys

Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.title: Modeling the CNOT gate in Germanium double quantum dots
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.abstract: We model a controlled-NOT (CNOT) gate mediated by exchange interactions in a realistic Ge/GeSi hole spin-qubit device. We use for that purpose a computationally efficient framework based on a compact dressed basis of many-body singlet and triplet states, which enables fast time-dependent simulations that would be prohibitive within a conventional configuration-interaction approach. We discuss the dominant sources of infidelity in ideal (noise-free) devices. On the one hand, the nonadiabaticity of the tunnel barrier ramps, enhanced by the transverse component of the exchange interaction, imposes limits on the speed of the CNOT gate. On the other hand, the AC Stark shift of the conditional resonance and the off-resonant driving of the complementary transition can significantly degrade the gate fidelity and call for a careful optimization of the driving conditions. Finally, we investigate the impact of quasi-static charge noise on the fidelity of the CNOT gate. We find that the capture of charges near the qubits can strongly disrupt the conditional operation, while the nanometer-scale motion of charges results in a loss of fidelity that sensitively depends on the position and strength of the corresponding dipole. Our results quantify the requirements on barrier control, microwave driving, and charge-noise stability for high-fidelity two-qubit operations in Ge/GeSi hole-spin qubits.

Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.title: Concentration quenching resistant violet-blue TADF OLEDs via indirect conformal distributions tuning in solid-state
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.authors: Hong-Ji Tan, Guo-Xi Yang, Jie-Rong Yu, Zhi-Qiang Long, Qing-Xiao Tong, Ze-Lin Zhu, Yin-Xuan Zhang, Daniel M. Dawson, Sharon E. Ashbrook, Shi-Jian Su, Jing-Xin Jian, Eli Zysman-Colman, Chun-Sing Lee
Germanium and Sn-Ge Epitaxy.abstract: Controlling conformation distributions is the key to manipulate material properties of multi-conformal molecules. Distinct from previous strategy with direct change or impact on the flexible groups, we tune the conformation distribution through changing peripheral groups to influence their intermolecular interactions. Two blue violet TADF emitters, namely tert -butyl substituted 5-(2,12-di-tert-butyl-5,9-dioxa-13b-boranaphtho[3,2,1-de]anthracen-7-yl)−10,10-diphenyl-5,10-dihydrodibenzo[b,e][1,4]azagermine (TDBA-PAG) and cumenyl substituted 5-(2,12-bis(2-phenylpropan-2-yl)−5,9-dioxa-13b-boranaphtho[3,2,1-de]anthracen-7-yl)−10,10-diphenyl-5,10-dihydrodibenzo[b,e][1,4]azagermine (TPDBA-PAG) were designed and synthesized. With the same germanium-integrated donor, the two compounds show similar emission properties in solution with calculated conformation dominantly of their quasi-axial (QA) forms (> 97%). However, TPDBA-PAG presents a lower QA ratio compared with TDBA-PAG, which endows the former with more pronounced TADF emission, higher emission efficiency and reduced concentration quenching phenomena in solid state. As a result, TPDBA-PAG performed as one of the best non-doped and doped violet-blue emitters and successfully sensitized MesB-DIDOBNA-N to achieve record high EQE max of 24.7% at 406 nm, making significant progress in NUV OLEDs.

Planar Josephson Junctions.title: Carrier-Induced and Coherent-Phonon-Controlled Band Renormalization in Quasi-One-Dimensional α-Bi4Br4
Planar Josephson Junctions.authors: Peng Tan, Yuantao Chen, Yuqi Zhang, Hanyan Cheng, Guoyu Xian, Ming Cheng, Minghong Sun, Jiaxin Yin, Feifan Wang, Yaxian Wang, Yanjun Liu, Mingyuan Huang, Zhiwei Wang, Yugui Yao, Sheng Meng, Li Huang, Yanan Dai
Planar Josephson Junctions.abstract: Directional control of band structures at ultrafast time scales is a key requirement for nanoscale optoelectronics. Here, we realize cooperative band engineering in the quasi-one-dimensional (quasi-1D) van der Waals topological insulator α-Bi4Br4 through joint carrier-phonon band renormalization. Femtosecond excitation drives quasi-1D carrier accumulation, generating a strongly nonlinear many-body band renormalization that redshifts an optical transition by up to ∼25 meV, with >90% polarization anisotropy. Superimposed Ag coherent phonons further modulate the same transition by ∼1 meV on intrinsic lattice time scales. By implementing phase-controlled dual-pump excitation, we achieve deterministic and reversible positioning of the renormalized band edge with ∼100 μeV precision within a ∼1.5 meV tuning window. First-principles calculations with charge-neutral photoexcitation constraints qualitatively reproduce the carrier-induced narrowing of the relevant interband transition, while phonon-mode analysis reveals that coherent Ag phonons modulate the same transition through interchain hopping and orbital polarization. These results establish cooperative carrier-phonon band renormalization as a scalable, all-optical mechanism for ultrafast, polarization-sensitive band engineering in quasi-1D van der Waals nanomaterials, enabling dynamically reconfigurable optoelectronic functionality.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Magnetotransport experiments on side-contacted topological insulator three-terminal Josephson junctions
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Christoph Wassmer, Ella Nikodem, Oliver Breunig, Yongjian Wang, Yoichi Ando, Jakob Schluck
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Multiterminal Josephson junctions have recently attracted substantial attention. The ability to study Andreev bound states in a multi-phase parameter space opens up exciting avenues for generating topologically non-trivial phases in superconducting devices. A particularly interesting case is the trijunction based on a topological insulator (TI), which is predicted to host Majorana zero modes for suitable phase configurations (Fu and Kane, PRL 2008). Here we turn to the platform of the side-contacted TI trijunction and present experimental evidence for a multiterminal Josephson effect. We study the transport properties and find typical features of a two-dimensional critical current contour (CCC) as well as bias regimes in which only a single junction remains dissipationless. We pay particular attention to these features and study the effects of magnetic fields on single junctions within the trijunction, where, depending on the field direction, the supercurrents show Fraunhofer patterns, SQUID oscillations, or a monotonic decay. We find good agreement with semiclassical simulations for a single TI junction that take into account the top and bottom surface states. We observe pronounced non-convex shape deformations of the CCC under perpendicular magnetic fields that reflect the flux buildup in the loop formed by our trijunctions and provide a simple model sufficient to explain the observed effect. Our results provide the foundations for future studies of Majorana zero modes on this platform.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Proximity-Induced Giant Majorana Spin Response in a UTe$_2$-Metal Film Heterostructure
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Jushin Tei, Makoto Shimizu, Yukio Tanaka, Satoshi Fujimoto, Takeshi Mizushima
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: We establish an experimentally accessible route to identifying Majorana surface states through their intrinsic Ising spin response, using UTe$_2$ as a concrete platform. The key is to extend the Majorana correlations into an adjacent metallic film via the superconducting proximity effect, thereby making the otherwise surface-localized response accessible to NMR measurements. Remarkably, disorder further sharpens the Majorana signature: impurity scattering suppresses the conventional $p$-wave proximity correlations while preserving the Majorana contribution, yielding a giant Ising-anisotropic enhancement of the NMR relaxation rate. This approach also offers a powerful means to distinguish among candidate pairing symmetries.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Continuous tuning of quantum critical behavior in hybrid Josephson junction arrays
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: E. Fugl, L. L. Olsen, S. Sasmal, M. Efthymiou-Tsironi, G. Nagda, F. Krizek, L. Casparis, S. Vaitiekėnas
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: We report finite-temperature scaling of voltage-driven quantum phase transitions in hybrid Josephson junction arrays. A dual-gate geometry separately tunes interisland coupling and proximity-induced superconductivity, providing access to superconducting, insulating, and metallic transport regimes. The critical resistivity and scaling exponent evolve continuously with electrostatic tuning. Where the three regimes converge, the critical resistivity approaches $h/4e^2$, consistent with the self-dual limit, while the scaling exponent approaches the quantum-percolation estimate. Tuning toward stronger insulating behavior raises the critical resistivity and shifts the scaling exponent toward the classical-percolation value, while both parameters decrease toward the metallic regime. These results connect scaling regimes previously reported in different two-dimensional superconducting systems through continuous electrostatic control.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Proximity-Induced Charge Transfer, Strain, and Possible Magnetic Exchange in Graphene/CrSBr Heterostructure
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Asish K. Kundu, Anil Rajapitamahuni, Niraj Aryal, Turgut Yilmaz, Margalit L. Feuer, Suji Park, Houk Jang, Abhay Pasupathy, Xavier Roy, Jerzy T. Sadowski, Elio Vescovo
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Stacking van der Waals materials provides a powerful route to engineer emergent electronic and magnetic behaviors through proximity-driven interactions. The graphene/CrSBr heterostructure has emerged as a compelling platform in this frontier, exhibiting exotic macroscopic responses (including uniaxial surface-plasmon-polariton propagation and an unconventional quantum Hall effect) indicative of strong interfacial electronic and magnetic coupling. However, a microscopic electronic landscape governing these phenomena has remained elusive. Here, we provide a comprehensive spectroscopic characterization of the graphene/CrSBr interface using a combination of angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), low-energy electron microscopy (LEEM), and density functional theory. We resolve a massive redistribution of interfacial charge that concurrently hole-dopes graphene and populates the quasi-one-dimensional spin-polarized conduction band of CrSBr, leading to interfacial metallization. Furthermore, electronic structure of CrSBr exhibits strong momentum-dependent renormalization distinct from conventional charge doping, and theoretical modeling supported by Raman spectroscopy points to additional interfacial compressive strain. In addition, ARPES reveals a splitting-like feature in the graphene Dirac cone consistent with spin degeneracy lifting, providing possible evidence of magnetic proximity coupling. These findings provide crucial microscopic insight into the system’s optical and transport responses and establish graphene/CrSBr as a versatile platform for charge-transfer control, strain-driven band engineering, magnetic-proximity coupling, and directionally confined excitations for next-generation spintronic and nanophotonic devices.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Andreev-Enhanced Conductance in a Bilayer Graphene Quantum Point Contact
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Emma Horgan, Bernd Aichner, Nadine Omar, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Luca Banszerus
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Quantum point contacts provide a platform for probing mode-dependent Andreev reflection. Here, we demonstrate Andreev-enhanced conductance in a gate-defined bilayer graphene quantum point contact coupled to a superconducting aluminum electrode. Electrostatic gating enables sequential mode occupation, verified by normal-state conductance quantization. In the superconducting state, the conductance is enhanced within the conductance plateaus, while the enhancement decreases between plateaus, consistent with the nonlinear transmission dependence of Andreev reflection. The enhancement yields effective transmission probabilities up to 0.9, and extends over a bias window of approximately 140 $μ$V, which we associate with a proximity-induced superconducting gap, close to the gap of the aluminum film. For in-plane fields, the enhancement persists up to the critical field, and the bias window follows the spectral gap predicted by Abrikosov-Gor'kov theory. In contrast, perpendicular fields suppress the enhancement approximately linearly from zero field, deviating from homogeneous pair breaking and indicative of flux penetration.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Coherent Electronic Lensing in Proximitized Graphene
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Ivan Villani, Samuele Fracassi, Niccolò Traverso Ziani, Maura Sassetti, Matteo Carrega, Vaidotas Mišeikis, Camilla Coletti, Fabio Beltram, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Sergio Pezzini, Stefan Heun
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Spatially resolved control of coherent electron transport offers a route to understanding and engineering interference phenomena in hybrid superconducting devices. Here, we use Scanning Gate Microscopy (SGM) to investigate Fabry-Pérot (FP) interference in the n-p-n cavity of a ballistic graphene Josephson junction. Spatial maps of the superconducting switching current and normal-state conductance reveal circular interference fringes arising from two distinct effects of the SGM tip potential. A global shift of the Fermi wave vector modulates the FP resonances of the cavity, while a local perturbation produces additional oscillations that persist at fixed Fermi wave vector as the tip bias is varied. An analytical model identifies the origin of this local response with coherent electron lensing, in which the tip modifies the phase accumulated along interfering trajectories. The measured fringe patterns in the switching current indicate that this mechanism affects superconducting transport, consistent with tip-induced shifts of the resonance conditions for Andreev bound states. These results establish SGM as a tunable local lens for controlling interference in superconducting ballistic graphene devices.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Inductorless fast phase logic: Enabling two-order-of-magnitude density scaling for superconductor VLSI
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Sasan Razmkhah, Massoud Pedram, Douglas Scott Holmes
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Fast phase logic (FPL) is a novel digital superconductor electronic (SCE) logic family that employs multiple junction types, including switching 0-Josephson junctions (0-JJs), non-switching 0-JJ stacks, and π-JJs. FPL enables flexible, automatable cell layouts, faster pulse propagation, reduced bias current via phaseshifting π-JJs, and minimized inductive loops, thereby reducing susceptibility to trapped flux and crosstalk.A fabrication process to support FPL is proposed. NbTiN superconductors offer small grain sizes, smooth surfaces, and thermal stability up to 400 ○ C, while high-Jc, self-shunted JJs enable compact devices. AlN dielectrics provide good crystal matching to NbTiN, improving superconducting properties. Projections indicate that FPL, combined with the proposed process, can achieve a two-order-of-magnitude increase in integration density over conventional RSFQ logic and a five-fold reduction in supply current. The increased density reduces latency and improves computational throughput, while NbTiN-based devices provide higher output voltage and impedance, improving compatibility with CMOS circuits. Further fabrication advancements, such as higher-Jc NbTiN-based JJs, higher processing temperatures, and stacked JJ structures, could enhance FPL implementation and scalability toward very large-scale integration (VLSI). FPL has the potential to significantly advance SCE technology, with near-term applications in accelerator cores for signal processing and artificial intelligence, and long-term potential in supercomputing. Its advantages are evaluated through an architectural study of a fast Fourier transform (FFT) circuit, with comparisons to CMOS and SFQ technologies for digital electronics.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Local Broadband Gigahertz Spectroscopy via SQUID-on-Tip DC Readout
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Senne Vervoort, Lukas Nulens, Julia Baumgarten, Daan B. Boltje, Jessalyn DeVine, Alejandro V. Silhanek, Joris Van de Vondel, Kaveh Lahabi
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Superconducting microwave circuits are shaped by their local electromagnetic environment, yet standard microwave measurements do not resolve the local fields and device features that govern their behavior. Here, we combine microwave spectroscopy, nanoscale magnetic sensing, and topographic imaging in a single tapping-mode SQUID-on-tip microscope. The nonlinear Josephson response converts local GHz excitations into Shapiro steps, enabling quantitative measurements of microwave frequency signals and their excitation strength using only DC readout. Applied to a superconducting coplanar waveguide resonator, local spectroscopy reproduces the power-dependent resonance and nonlinear bifurcation observed in microwave transmission measurements. Spatially resolved measurements map the microwave response while simultaneously recording topography and static magnetic features, including vortices and Meissner screening currents. Electromagnetic simulations reveal how coupling through the superconducting probe leads limits spatial resolution and guides localized detector designs. Together, these capabilities establish a platform for correlating microwave circuit dynamics with the local structural and magnetic environment of superconducting devices.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Nano-Nb Superconducting 3D Josephson Junctions Arrays in Cu-Normal Matrix: Superconducting Phase Coherence and Quantum Fluctuations Properties
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: R. L. de Almeida, J. Albino Aguiar, J. A. H. Coaquira
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: To address the complex interplay of microstructural evolution, phase separation, superconductivity coherence and quantum fluctuations, we prepared Cuxwt%Nb series of granular samples by rapidly cooling, where the niobium concentration varied (x = 3, 5, 15, 20). By employing this method, we successfully obtained samples characterized by well-defined precipitates of niobium, featuring regular sizes and grain spacing. The goal was to establish a systematic and robust method approach for obtaining samples with different of sub-micrometric precipitates distributions but also to investigate their superconducting properties. Structural characterization by optical and Scanning Electron Microscopy, dc Mdc[H,T] ac inductive , as well the magneto-transport measures rhodc[H,T], Rdc[V,I.H,T], I[V,H,T] and [H,T,I] were done. Also, using a micro Hall sensor with 10 measuring transverse voltage bridges regularly distributed, we were able to obtain the real external applied magnetic field value inside of the chamber sample space. Thus e studied the dependence of configuration of the Nb grains in the superconducting coupling order parameter properties that connects the grains superconductors to the normal Cu matrix. We verify through magnetization and transport measures the signature of the double transition. This, when we apply current of different intensities, in the transport measures, and different field values, in the inductive measures. This behavior is an indication that our system is made up of by a collection of superconducting grains immersed in a well-organized in a non-superconducting matrix. The results indicate that the superconducting properties of these systems are manifested usually through two transition temperatures Tc(H) e TcJ(H).

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: GaS–SnSSe heterostructure: A strain-tunable direct bandgap Rashba semiconductor
Berry curvature dipole circuit quantum electrodynamics
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Oles Matsyshyn, Valla Fatemi, Justin C. W. Song
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Quantum three-wave mixing is an important resource in superconducting quantum circuits. The traditional implementation uses Josephson junction arrays and is activated by magnetic flux. Here we introduce the Berry curvature dipole (BCD) quantum circuit element, which achieves quantum three-wave mixing without breaking time-reversal symmetry. This quantum three-wave mixing results from the BCD nonlinear Hall effect in noncentrosymmetric quantum materials taken to a dissipationless, quantum coherent few-photon regime. We show how nonlinear Hall materials can be integrated to superconducting microwave circuits to accomplish multiphoton vacuum Rabi splittings and dynamical stabilization of bosonic Schrödinger cat states. Such BCD circuit quantum electrodynamics are a concrete exemplar of a physical resource for quantum information processing enabled by nonlinear response in quantum materials.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Magnetic Imaging with High Spatial Resolution Using a Single Niobium-Nitride-Based Three-Dimensional Nanobridge Junction
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Yinping Pan, Yue Wang, Xinxin Fan, Xu Liu, Shirui Liu, Xiaoyu Liu, Ling Wu, Lu Zhang, Wei Peng, Jie Ren, Jiamin Xiong, Hao Li, Lixing You, Zhen Wang, Lei Chen
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: The nanobridge junctions (NBJs) allow the miniaturization of the Superconducting Quantum Interference Device (SQUID) and improve the spatial resolution of scanning SQUID microscopy. However, the SQUID loop diameter imposed a fundamental limit on the resolution. In this work, we proposed a single niobium-nitride-based three-dimensional nanobridge junction (NbN-3D-NBJ) alternative to the nanoSQUID for high-resolution magnetic imaging. The critical current of an NbN-3D-NBJ showed an nearly monotonic dependence on the external magnetic field, enabling nanoscale mapping of the magnetic field distribution by measuring the junction's critical current with an intrinsic noise level of 100 nT/Hz^1/2. Using a NbN-3D-NBJ probe, we successfully imaged an Abrikosov vortex in a niobium film with a minimal full width at half maxima (FWHM) of 530 nm, constrained by the distance from the junction to the probe tip edge. Furthermore, we resolved 80 nm spacings between the superconducting nanowires utilizing a second probe with an optimized junction-to-tip distance. Thus, the single 3D NbN NBJ probe has been demonstrated as an effective approach for magnetic imaging with ultra-high spatial resolution.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Spin Relaxation and Electrical Control of Spin Transport in Few-Layer $T_{\rm d}$-MoTe$_2$
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: T. Wakamura, M. Hashisaka, M. Bard, S. Okazaki, T. Sasagawa, T. Taniguchi, K. Watanabe, K. Muraki, N. Kumada
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: We report electrical tuning of spin relaxation in atomically thin $T_{\rm d}$-MoTe$_2$, a representative low-symmetry transition metal dichalcogenide. Weak antilocalization measurements reveal strong spin--orbit interaction with spin--orbit lengths of tens of nanometers, consistent with recent theoretical predictions. Despite the semimetallic nature of $T_{\rm d}$-MoTe$_2$, in the ultrathin limit the spin--orbit scattering time can be tuned electrostatically by up to threefold. We further investigate vertical electric field effects on the spin--orbit length and time, and demonstrate the modulation of the Rashba parameters. Relation between spin--orbit scattering time and the diffusion coefficient indicates that spin relaxation is governed by the D'yakonov--Perel' mechanism in both monolayer and bilayer $T_{\rm d}$-MoTe$_2$. These results establish few-layer $T_{\rm d}$-MoTe$_2$ as a platform for electrically tunable spin transport, thereby providing insight into spin relaxation in low-symmetry transition metal dichalcogenides.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Channel-Resolved Perturbative Analysis of Parameter-Spread Effects in rf-SQUID Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifiers
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Xinyu Wu, Wei-Wei Ling, Jianshe Liu
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Josephson traveling-wave parametric amplifiers (JTWPAs) are well suited to broadband amplification in superconducting quantum readout, but their long nonlinear transmission lines are sensitive to fabrication-induced parameter spread. We develop a channel-resolved perturbative analysis for three-wave-mixing JTWPAs based on radio-frequency superconducting quantum interference devices (rf-SQUIDs), separating the effects of parameter variations into linear scattering, phase mismatch, and direct change in the quadratic coupling. A physical-cell Bloch projection resolves the local phase and scattering terms, while the rf-SQUID expansion gives the direct coupling variation. Their effects are quantified through average gain, gain ripple, and passive reflection. For the periodically loaded rf-SQUID JTWPA studied here, critical-current spread mainly affects the average gain through the nonlinear coupling, whereas loop-inductance and shunt-capacitance spreads contribute more strongly to ripple and reflection through linear scattering. Their relative importance also changes with the spatial correlation of the parameter variations. These results show that fabrication tolerances should be considered together with the relevant amplifier metric, clarifying how parameter variations influence the broadband gain response and reflection through distinct physical channels.

Josephson and Proximity Effects.title: Kineoelasticity and nonreciprocal phonons by Rashba-induced interfacial spin-lattice coupling
Structural supermodulation enables resonant Raman determination of crystalline orientation in Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8+x flakes
Josephson and Proximity Effects.authors: Flavia Lo Sardo, Tommaso Confalone, Shreya Kumbhakar, Genda Gu, Ahmad Omar, Christian G. F. Blum, Daniel Wolf, Davide Massarotti, Francesco Tafuri, Axel Lubk, Kornelius Nielsch, Nicola Poccia, Golam Haider
Josephson and Proximity Effects.abstract: Bi2Sr2CaCu2O8+x (Bi-2212) is a d-wave superconductor with unconventional properties intrinsic to the material itself. These properties are of growing interest for quantum technologies in electronics and photonics, and twisted Josephson junctions can make direct use of them. However, Bi-2212 is strongly anisotropic, and it is challenging to find its crystal axes in flakes in advance, which limits device engineering. Here, we show that polarized resonant Raman spectroscopy reveals the orientation of both the a and b axes of Bi-2212 optically and non-destructively. By correlating Laue diffraction, HAADF-STEM and polarized Raman scattering on the same bulk crystal, we assign the b axis, along which the incommensurate structural supermodulation propagates, to the intensity maximum of the 27 cm-1 supermodulation mode, which varies in counter-phase with the 118 cm-1 Bi/Sr mode, along the a axis. Multi-wavelength measurements (458, 532, 660 nm) show that resulting in-plane contrast peaks at 532 nm and nearly vanishes at 660 nm, indicating that the anisotropy originates from an electronic resonance induced by the supermodulation. Using this resonance, we determine the crystallographic axes of exfoliated flakes and access their symmetry channels, providing a rapid orientation tool for cuprate van der Waals heterostructures.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Majorana Zero Modes in Fractional Vortices
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Lecheng Fang, Haotian Li, Haijiao Ji, Quanxin Hu, Hong Ding, Noah F. Q. Yuan
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: Majorana zero modes (MZMs) are promising for topological quantum computation, with vortices in topological superconductors serving as a leading platform. Recent experiments show that integer Abrikosov vortices in iron-based superconductors can split into fractional vortices (FVs) carrying fractional flux quanta. We show that due to topological protection, MZMs hosted by FVs are spatially unfolded over the FV cores, while fermionic bound states remain localized at individual FV cores. This yields zero-bias conductance peaks in both local tunneling and nonlocal crossed Andreev reflection, offering an alternative MZM signature.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Parity-Resolved Many-Body Kinetics of a Topological Qubit under Nonequilibrium Phonon Pulses
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: Phonon bursts from ionizing radiation cause correlated errors in superconducting quantum processors. We study prescribed nonequilibrium phonon pulses in a Majorana qubit formed by two $2\,μ\mathrm{m}$ proximitized nanowires. Combining the lattice Lutchyn--Oreg model, microscopic electron--phonon coupling, and parity-resolved many-body dynamics, we track excitation, relaxation, and logical coherence. Without quasiparticle escape, recombination restores the initial Majorana occupations in about 130 ns, while phonons exchanged during excitation and recovery can retain logical-state information, leaving permanent coherence loss. For mirror-symmetric wires, the fractional coherence loss per wire is 0.75--1.0 times the excitation probability averaged over the two logical states, even at zero Majorana splitting; breaking mirror symmetry can suppress dephasing at small splitting. Factorized Boltzmann kinetics neglects quasiparticle correlations and overestimates residual parity flips. At equal deposited energy density, phonon spectra yield different excitation probabilities and coherence losses. Comparisons with Kitaev chains matched to the wire's gap and Majorana decay length reveal that low electron density suppresses excitation by energetic phonons, whereas hard-wall boundaries in a high-density control increase excitation efficiency by a factor of $5\times10^4$ relative to the wire for pulses centered at 1 meV. Magnetic-field and chemical-potential tuning yield different phonon sensitivities at the same bulk gap through changes in spin and electron--hole structure. Including hybrid states' semiconductor weights reduces near-threshold excitation rates fourfold when the tunnel coupling equals the parent superconducting gap. Our framework connects phonon spectra to leakage, poisoning, and coherence loss to guide Majorana-device design.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Topological Quantum Spin Liquids in a Ladder with Majorana fermions and p-wave Superconductivity
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Magali Korolev, Fan Yang, Erik S. Sørensen, Karyn Le Hur
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: In this article, we address the possibility of topological quantum spin liquids with only short-range (spin) correlations in the whole phase diagram in a ladder system, through an exactly solvable model which represents a generalization of the two-dimensional Kitaev honeycomb spin model to a ribbon geometry. This system gives rise to $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge fields emerging in a static way in the ground state through Majorana fermions which then produce either $0$ or $π$ flux. Through a quantum field theory perspective, mathematical and Density Matrix Renormalization Group results, we present our progress on the geometrical, topological and physical classification of this model through observables navigating on the whole phase diagram presenting three spin-liquid phases with a spin gap and a metallic phase in the sense of Majorana fermions. We propose a bulk-edge correspondence revealing the presence of protected zero-energy Majorana fermions at the edge in the phases with a gap and revealing also the presence of itinerant Majorana fermions in the bulk in the topological liquid phase. The proposed approach allows us to distinguish between properties of the brickwall ladder giving rise to a special line and those of the square ladder allowing for the gapless Majorana liquid phase. This model gives some hope on finding solutions for topological quantum spin models, e.g. with $π$ flux, on a square lattice geometry. This approach also allows for a correspondence onto models of topological superconductivity.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Quantifying Majorana-qubit stability through parity-resolved Rabi dynamics
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Yu Zhang, Jiayi Chen, Jie Liu, X. C. Xie

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Finite-Depth Interfacial Coupling in Metal/Topological Insulator van der Waals Heterostructures
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Yin-Song Liao, Hsin-Hsien Chan, Ruei-Yu Wang, Han-Wei Tsai, Hsun-Ting Hsieh, Cheng-Maw Cheng, Jyh-Pin Chou, Meng-Kai Lin
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: Metal/topological insulator van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures offer a platform for engineering emergent quantum states beyond isolated layers. While proximity effects in covalently bonded systems are well studied, coupling depth across vdW interfaces remains unclear. Using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy and first-principles calculations, we investigate the thickness dependence of TiTe2/Bi2Te3 electronic states. Despite nominally weak vdW bonding, the buried interface induces emergent bands and splitting near a band crossing, consistent with hybridization. Interface-induced features persist in the bilayer, while band evolution nearly saturates in thicker films. Even at four layers, the electronic structure does not simply recover to the intrinsic TiTe2 limit, consistent with finite-depth coupling that substantially reshapes the overlayer bands. Charge redistribution and a moiré-modulated interfacial potential contribute to this reconstruction. Finite-depth coupling may be a hallmark of strongly coupled vdW heterostructures and guide topological and quantum electronic device design.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Chiral superconductivity on a closed Klein bottle: a chirality wall and its Majorana seam spectrum
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: We study a spinless $π$-flux lattice superconductor whose normal-state momentum-space fundamental domain is a Klein bottle. Within this model, a glide lift and a hidden antiunitary symmetry independently force the Bogoliubov--de Gennes (BdG) Chern number to vanish. A diagonal pairing breaks the antiunitary obstruction exactly when its real part is nonzero; this is necessary, not sufficient, for a chiral phase. We derive explicit Pfaffians determining Chern parity and identify three analytic families of gap closings in a real-pairing section. For a chiral state on a closed real-space Klein bottle, the prescribed pairing and gluing produce a $ΔC=2$ chirality wall. A translation-invariant unfolding resolves two co-propagating Majorana branches. Their finite-size levels depend on circumference and holonomy; the near-zero pair is lifted at first order by allowed local seam perturbations. A cut-cylinder control has the same low-energy channel count, so gluing reconnects existing gapless content. We also distinguish literal gluing from deck projection: particle--hole symmetry exchanges the deck eigenblocks, precluding their interpretation as independent BdG quotient Hamiltonians. The contribution is a model-specific account of pairing compatibility and closed-surface seam spectra. The energy cost is evaluated for a fixed pairing background; neither a protected zero mode nor a self-consistent wall solution is claimed.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Nonuniform superconducting states from Majorana flat bands
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.authors: Sushanth Varada, Aksel Kobiałka, Ankita Bhattacharya, Patric Holmvall, Annica M. Black-Schaffer

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Field theory of competing phases in the interacting Kitaev chain
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: We study the interacting Kitaev chain with nearest-neighbor interactions and finite chemical potential using a combination of bosonization and density-matrix renormalization-group calculations. Focusing away from special exactly solvable lattice limits, we develop a continuum field-theoretic description of the generic finite-density interacting regime, where doping nonperturbatively modifies the competition between superconducting pairing and commensurate charge ordering. We show that the phase diagram consists of an intermediate incommensurate Luttinger liquid between the topological superconducting and commensurate charge-density-wave Mott phases, as well as a trivial band-insulating regime at large chemical potential. The commensurate--incommensurate and incommensurate--topological-superconducting phase boundaries are governed by Pokrovsky--Talapov and Berezinskii--Kosterlitz--Thouless criticality, respectively. We analyze the interacting topological superconducting regime and its boundary excitations. At the semiclassical level, and explicitly in the free-fermion boundary theory, the topological phase supports exponentially localized Majorana edge modes at interfaces between topological and trivial regions. We also construct a dual continuum fermionic representation in which this topological bulk sector is described instead by conventional symmetry breaking. This gives a continuum version of the SPT--SSB correspondence between different fermionic representations. Overall, our results provide an analytical description of one-dimensional interacting topological superconductors, from the competition between topology and commensurability and the resulting quantum criticality to the dual symmetry-breaking description of the topological phase.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Layer-Parity Control of the Superconducting Diode Effect in Monolayer NbSe$_2$
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: The superconducting diode effect is often associated with finite-momentum pairing, although model studies indicate that rectification reflects the asymmetry of the free energy about its minimum rather than the equilibrium pair momentum itself. Using a Wannier-based, self-consistent finite-$\mathbf Q$ Bogoliubov-de Gennes approach with a Fermi-surface-adaptive quadrature that converges the critical currents, we show that the layer parity and orientation of magnetic proximity select the diode response of monolayer NbSe$_2$. For in-plane exchange, the equilibrium pair momentum $\mathbf Q_{\rm eq}$ and the diode efficiency are both linear in the layer-odd exchange contrast: parallel proximity on the two Se sublayers is reciprocal, and antiparallel proximity doubles the response. An out-of-plane component separates the two observables. It leaves $\mathbf Q_{\rm eq}$ nearly unchanged but, through pair breaking, suppresses the efficiency by more than an order of magnitude and, at low temperature, reverses it. Purely out-of-plane exchange, for which $C_3$ symmetry forbids a helical term, keeps $\mathbf Q_{\rm eq}=0$ yet produces a trigonal diode effect, controlled by the layer-even exchange and larger than the in-plane one above $0.65$~meV at low temperature. Magnetic layer parity thus selects between a helical and a trigonal diode channel. The trigonal channel is an intrinsic, symmetry-allowed contribution to the field-free rectification reported in NbSe$_2$/CrBr$_3$ and predicts that two-sided out-of-plane proximity cancels it when antiparallel and, at the same exchange per layer, enhances it about fourfold when parallel, in the computed range.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Exploring entropic orders: High-temperature continuous symmetry breaking and topological order
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: High temperature is usually expected to destroy order: as the Gibbs state approaches the infinite-temperature limit, it becomes an equal-weight ensemble over all states and the system is generically disordered. Recent works showed that entropic order can violate this expectation through coupling to bosons in classical lattice models and quantum field theories, where the ordered states have higher entropy. Here we present new analytic methods for constructing quantum lattice models that exhibit entropic orders. In particular, we construct quantum lattice models with continuous symmetry breaking at high temperature in 1 + 1 dimensions and clarify how entropic order can evade the Hohenberg-Mermin-Wagner theorems. We also construct high-temperature entropic p + i p chiral topological superconducting states in 2 + 1 dimensions with temperature-independent anyon correlation functions. In addition, we obtain a broad family of high-temperature entropic nonchiral topological orders. We show that the entropic topological orders have strong higher-form symmetries at high temperature unlike the conventional topological orders, and the symmetry is spontaneously broken. These results follow from two general constructions that couple a given lattice model with a low-temperature ordered phase either to ordered bosons, or for local commuting-projector Hamiltonians, to more general bosonic degrees of freedom.

Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.title: Gravitational anomaly spectroscopy of a Kitaev spin liquid
Majorana and Topological Superconductivi.abstract: The chiral central charge $c$ measures the gravitational anomaly of a two-dimensional topological phase. It fixes the heat current carried along the edge. So far, it has been accessed through thermal transport, where phonons complicate the signal, or through wave-function probes that need a pure ground state. Here we show that $c$ is a spectroscopic quantity of the edge. A weak modulation of the edge couplings that travel along the edge is absorbed according to the Virasoro algebra. Normalized by the response to a static change of the same couplings, the absorbed weights obey $D_n=2n\langle L_0\rangle+\frac{c}{12}(n^3-n)$, so that $\mathcal{C}\equiv2D_2-4D_1=c$ in any state of the ideal edge theory, thermal or not. The central charge thus appears in transition weights, although it cancels from excitation gaps. The ratio of line weights with and without a vison in the bulk, $Λ=4h_σ/c$, needs no calibration and fixes the conformal spin $h_σ$ of the non-Abelian Ising anyon. For the Kitaev honeycomb spin liquid we find $\mathcal{C}=0.49999$ and $h_σ=0.06250$ on 7168 spins. Calibrating with the shift of the measured line itself gives $c$ within about $1\%$ on 96 spins and within $1\%$ under $20\%$ random coupling errors. Interacting edge Majoranas in a fixed flux sector, treated with DMRG, keep $\mathcal{C}$ within $1.5\%$ while the edge velocity changes by $\pm13\%$. An exact simulation of a quantum-processor protocol, including the native Floquet circuit, returns $c$ within $3.5\%$ on 96 to 600 spins.

Altermagnets and Novel Heterostructures.title: Steering and local tunneling signatures of Majorana corner modes in altermagnetic Josephson junctions
